title: POC weekly - latency tuning (TTFT / streaming / kernels) - Rivermark
summary: Weekly POC sync to review latency benchmarks and next tuning steps. TTFT improved with streaming and prefix caching but 99p tail still elevated due to long sequence spikes and batching policy. Agreed to run kernel-level bench with varied sequence lengths, test adaptive batching, and perform on-prem kernel comparison. Next call scheduled for 2027-12-14.
action_items: Priya Singh: run kernel micro-bench (CUTLASS vs Triton vs Redwood tiled) at seq len 64/256/512/1024 and share results - due 2027-12-14
Jason Kim (Rivermark): provide production seq length histogram & top-10 worst prompts by 2027-12-09
Alex Moore: share updated benchmark spreadsheet + canary rollout plan and suggested autoscale thresholds - due 2027-12-09
Maya Lopez: enable dev cluster KV cache pre-warm and report cold-start TTFT numbers - due 2027-12-10
next_steps: Alex to send kernel benchmark template and spreadsheet
Priya to run micro-bench and update with 99p latencies
Customer to provide real request histograms
Schedule on-prem kernel comparison window next week
Confirm canary rollout parameters once benches look stable
transcript: [00:00] Alex: ok, welcome everyone, thanks for joining, this is the weekly poc sync for latency tuning; quick roll call?
[00:10] Tom: hey Alex, Tom here, Maya and Jason are on, Nina too
[00:15] Maya: hi all
[00:18] Jason: hi, Jason here
[00:22] Alex: cool, Priya from our side?
[00:25] Priya: yeah hey, Priya, i'll talk through the kernel tests and streaming tweaks we tried this week
[00:30] Alex: quick recap of numbers first - Priya you wanna give the headline?

[00:36] Priya: sure, so we re-ran the benchmark against your dev workload, default model config vs streaming enabled with prefix cache; TTFT improved from avg ~320ms down to ~170-190ms for typical short requests, 50th/90th good, but 99p is still spikey, around 1.3s in some runs
[00:51] Jason: those 99p spikes correlate with long sequences? we do see occasional 700-1000 token prompts for retrospectives
[00:58] Priya: yep exactly, the distribution matters a lot; most requests are 32-128 tokens but those long ones blow out CPU/GPU scheduling and kv cache thrash
[01:10] Alex: just to be clear, TTFT here is time-to-first-token measured from request arrival to first token out, right?
[01:15] Priya: yep TTFT as measured at our edge; streaming chunk size and pre-warm helped a lot — smaller first chunk reduced first-token latency but increased total tokens emitted overhead slightly
[01:25] Maya: there's some fuzzy words in the spreadsheet, looks like 'Redwood Dedicat' was written, i assume you mean Dedicated cluster?
[01:31] Alex: yes, that's a transcribe typo — we tested on dedicated-like instance pools in dev to emulate your reserved capacity
[01:36] Jason: curious about kernels — you mentioned CUTLASS vs Triton, any clear winner?

[01:42] Priya: short answer: it depends. CUTLASS gave slightly better throughput at larger seq lengths, Triton kernels were better for medium seqs and lower memory pressure. Our tiled/custom kernel had best 99p on some configs but needs validation on your on-prem hw
[01:58] Tom: on-prem hw is older gen A100s, we also have a small cluster with L40s for burst. can you run the bench there?
[02:05] Priya: yes we can run on-prem comparison; need SSH info and a test window, and ideally a docker image. we'll put together a kernel bench template
[02:12] Alex: Jason, can you share the seq length histogram from production? that'll let us weight the bench accordingly
[02:18] Jason: yes, i'll pull and send, should have it by tomorrow
[02:22] Maya: one observation — the worst tail seems linked to batching behaviour when concurrency spikes; batching groups long and short requests together and long ones push the batch duration up
[02:33] Priya: right, adaptive batching thresholds help — we tried a threshold that prefers latency SLO over batch size if expected seq len high, that reduced 99p by ~200ms in dev
[02:44] Alex: can you explain the adaptive batching setting quickly?
[02:47] Priya: sure, we set a sequence-length aware bucketer so it won't batch short requests with a waiting long request beyond X ms; also we cap batch size for streams to avoid long tail buildup
[02:58] Jason: ok, makes sense. question: will prefix/KV caching help those long ones? i thought cache is mostly helpful for repeated prefixes

[03:06] Priya: it does when the prompt has common boilerplate; for one-off long prompts it helps less, but we can pre-warm KV cache for models that maintain session history so subsequent tokens have lower latency
[03:18] Nina: are we concerned about quantization here? we tried 4-bit in staging and saw accuracy drift

[03:23] Priya: quantization reduces memory and can improve throughput but it can impact output quality; for now we recommend 8-bit or mixed-precision for Rivermark until we validate quality on your eval set
[03:33] Alex: note for action, we'll run kernel micro-bench across seq lengths 64/256/512/1024 and include 99p latency column
[03:42] Maya: and please include cold-start TTFT vs warmed cache numbers, that's key for our interactive flows
[03:47] Priya: yes we'll capture cold vs warm, and streaming chunk sizes (we tried 8 token first chunk vs 32 token first chunk; 8 token lowered TTFT by ~60ms but increased network calls)
[04:00] Tom: tradeoff there is additional overhead on client side; may be ok for chat but not for single-turn search
[04:06] Alex: good point, we can recommend per-route configs—search endpoints get bigger first chunk, chat gets small first chunk
[04:12] Jason: curious about the 'redwood tiled kernel' you mentioned — is that something you ship or internal?

[04:17] Priya: it's our optimized tiled matmul path that reduces memory movement for longer sequences; stable in hosted and Dedicated but for Private we need to validate on your exact driver stack because sometimes cu-blass/cublas versions cause perf diffs (transcribe: cu-blass typo in notes)
[04:33] Maya: driver versions are a pain; we have R470 driver on A100 cluster, L40 cluster has newer
[04:38] Alex: we'll include driver matrix guidance in the benchmark template
[04:42] Priya: also note streaming implementation: we added a tiny prefetch to assemble first chunk earlier and use async io, that helped TTFT for short samples
[04:52] Jason: can you quantify the improvement on our workload?
[04:55] Priya: for your sampled dev traffic, median TTFT went 320 -> 180ms, 90p 560 -> 300ms, 99p 1.6s -> 1.3s but after adaptive batching and kernel tuning we're hitting ~1.0s 99p in some runs
[05:10] Tom: that's promising — still want 99p < 800ms ideally, but we accept iterative improvements
[05:16] Alex: agreed, target for pilot is 99p < 800ms for typical workload; for edge cases we want clear mitigation steps (rate-limit, route to background tier)
[05:25] Maya: next, can you share the canary rollout plan? we need to know thresholds to auto-fallback
[05:30] Alex: brief: start with 5% traffic, monitor TTFT and token cost delta; if 99p exceeds threshold or token cost > 20% we abort; after 24h look good, move to 25% then 100%
[05:42] Priya: we'll provide helm snippet and config for canary windows; also include autoscale policys and queue depth thresholds
[05:50] Jason: for on-prem benchmark, we prefer a small window during low traffic, can you coordinate next week?
[05:56] Priya: yes we'll propose windows in the spreadsheet
[06:00] Alex: ok let's recap actions and owners
[06:04] Alex: Priya to run kernel micro-bench and send results; Jason to send seq hist; Maya to enable KV pre-warm in dev and report cold numbers; Alex to share benchmark spreadsheet and canary plan
[06:15] Nina: quick question — security docs, we still need the SOC2 questionnaire answers, any update?
[06:20] Alex: i'll share our SOC2 and encryption/KMS notes after the call, plus network diagrams
[06:25] Tom: great, thanks. when's next sync?
[06:28] Alex: same time next week, 2027-12-14 14:00 UTC, i'll send calendar invite
[06:33] Maya: thanks everyone
[06:35] Jason: thanks
[06:37] Priya: thanks, bye
[06:40] Alex: bye
